title: How Letters Get Spaced
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you drag letters to see why spacing follows white area, and when one pair still needs kerning.
pitch: Start by fixing an ugly word with a tracking slider and one kerning drag, then discover why the same distance between letter edges looks different for HH, HO and AV: what the eye reads is the white area. A ladder of small demos built on a typeface drawn in code lets the visitor space letters by area, watch the rhythm of a row of n and o, blur the text to see its grey tone, and learn which pairs spacing cannot fix.
firstMinute: The page opens on the word AVOID set with default spacing, with the gap between A and V shaded so the hole is visible, and a tracking slider plus a draggable pair handle. Dragging the V towards the A closes the hole and the shaded area number drops, which is the first success with no reading.
conceptsToLearn: Every letter sits in a box with a little space on each side; the gap you see between two letters is the sum of those two spaces
Tracking spaces a whole run of text equally; kerning adjusts the gap of one pair only
whyNow: Timeless: anyone who sets headlines, logos or slides meets uneven letter gaps. Type spacing is a niche most people have never been shown properly.

purposeDetail.concept: Letter spacing is set by the white area between letters, not by the distance between their edges; kerning is a patch for the few pairs that spacing cannot fix.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: People know the words kerning and tracking but rarely see how a type designer sets the space on each side of every letter first, or why diagonal and round letters break the rules.
purposeDetail.audience: Designers, students, slide-makers and curious readers; no design knowledge needed.
misconceptions: Kerning and tracking are the same thing (the page treats this as a common mix-up only as reported, not as a confirmed statistic).
Uneven spacing is fixed by adding kerning pairs everywhere.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Two pairs with identical edge-to-edge distance, H next to H and A next to V, look nothing alike, and the shaded white areas show why; closing the area, not the distance, evens the row.
demos: 1. Tracking against kerning: a slider moves every gap, a handle moves one pair.
2. Same distance, different area: shaded gaps for HH, HO, OO and AV with live area numbers.
3. Space by area: set one target area and see sidebearings computed for a small geometric typeface drawn from shapes, with an n-and-o rhythm strip.
4. Blur test: a squint slider shows the grey tone of a line before and after spacing.
5. What spacing cannot fix: AV, To and WA, where a hand-set kerning pair is the right tool.
checkQuestions: If you tighten every gap in a headline equally, are you tracking or kerning?
Which pair needs more care at equal edge distance: HH or AV, and why?
After spacing by area, one pair still looks open. What is the right fix?

research.summary: Verified by search only (no page opened). Two separate sources agree that type designers set each glyph's sidebearings first and add kerning only for pairs that spacing cannot fix. The fence-of-n method and the x-height zone are described by a Leiden thesis and a second article. An open spacing tool sets sidebearings from white area and says it does not kern. Definitions of kerning and tracking, the claim that they are often confused, the capitals that trap space and the even-grey goal were not confirmed by two separate results, so the page words them as general typographic practice or omits them. The typeface is drawn in code, so no font file is used.

sources.title: Bad Spacing (Monotype Foundry Support)
sources.snippet: Foundry guidance: spacing problems are not to be solved with kerning pairs; set each glyph's sidebearings first, then add kerning for specific exceptions; a round o should sit centred in its space.
sources.note: Re-found by my own search: the foundry's own support page gives the order sidebearings first, kerning second; round o sits centred in its space.

sources.title: FontLab TV: spacing letters from scratch
sources.snippet: Advises solving spacing with sidebearings wherever possible and reserving kerning for pairs nothing else can fix.
sources.note: Not re-found by my searches; FontLab's own help tutorial (source 10) was found saying the same, so this link is kept only as a lead.

sources.title: The Briem method and the geometry of nothing (FontLab blog)
sources.snippet: Treats spacing as setting rhythm and describes linking sidebearings of related letters to the n.
sources.note: Not re-found by my searches; the Briem-method wording is a lead only and the page does not rely on it.

sources.title: Leiden University thesis on letter spacing
sources.snippet: States that type designers often start with a fence of n or m and judge other letters against it, and that only the x-height zone matters for spacing roman lowercase.
sources.note: Found again by my search (two links to one thesis count once): fence of n or m, only the x-height zone matters for roman lowercase. Independent second source is source 11.

sources.title: A free tool for spacing fonts (HT Letterspacer)
sources.snippet: The tool's own site says it sets sidebearings from the white area in each glyph box using a few parameters, and that it does not kern.
sources.note: Re-found by my search; the tool's official site and tutorial state the area method and that it does not kern. The 'does not replace the designer's eye' wording was not seen and is dropped.

sources.title: Class 4 - Controlling Space, Leading, Tracking and Kerning (CUNY City Tech course)
sources.snippet: A design course page that treats kerning as pair adjustment and notes it is often confused with tracking.
sources.note: Not re-found by my searches (a different course page of that site surfaced); the claim that the two terms are often confused rests on nothing I saw, so it is dropped as a fact.

sources.title: Adventures in Space: Tracking (FontShop article on MyFonts)
sources.snippet: Says the two terms are frequently confused; kerning fixes a specific pair, tracking spaces a run of text as a design choice.
sources.note: Not re-found by my searches; the claim that the terms are frequently confused is not confirmed.

sources.title: Tracking vs Kerning vs Leading: the difference in 30 seconds (LS Graphics)
sources.snippet: Short explainer separating tracking (one value across a run of text) from kerning (one pair).
sources.note: Found in my search, but the search summary blended several results (also a Figma page and a studio blog), so I cannot tell which carried which sentence; definition stays unverified and the page words it in its own terms.

sources.title: Journal of Graphic Engineering and Design paper on letterspacing
sources.snippet: Journal article listing on letterspacing; the earlier dossier says it describes an even grey value as the goal.
sources.note: The article listing was found again, but I did not see the text about an even grey value, so that claim is unverified.

sources.title: Adventures in Space: Kerning (FontShop article on MyFonts)
sources.snippet: Search summary said sidebearings handle most issues but letters such as A, L, T, V, W and Y trap space so some pairs need kerning.
sources.note: Found by my search (clean address). A summary says most spacing is fixed with sidebearings but some capitals (A, L, T, V, W, Y) trap space; one result only, so unverified.

sources.title: FontLab in 8 days, Day 5: Social letters (FontLab help)
sources.snippet: Tutorial advises finishing spacing before starting kerning and adding kerning exceptions afterwards.
sources.note: Found by my search; the editor vendor's own tutorial agrees with the foundry page on the order of work.

sources.title: How to space a typeface (MyFonts)
sources.snippet: Article on spacing a typeface that also stresses the x-height zone and checking letters against n.
sources.note: Found by my search; independent of the Leiden thesis on the x-height point.

facts.claim: Foundry and editor guidance: fix spacing problems by adjusting each glyph's sidebearings first, and add kerning only afterwards for pairs that remain awkward.
Type designers commonly judge spacing against a fence of n or m letters, and for roman lowercase only the space inside the x-height zone matters for spacing.
An open area-based spacing tool sets sidebearings from the white area of each glyph box and does not kern.
As of 2026-10-13, per LS Graphics only: kerning adjusts the space of one pair, tracking changes spacing across a whole run of text. Not confirmed by a second separate result.
As of 2026-10-13, per FontShop (MyFonts) only: some capitals such as A, L, T, V, W and Y trap space that sidebearings cannot fully fix, so a few pairs need kerning. Not confirmed by a second result.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: see a flaw, move a handle or slider to remove it, read the number that changes, then answer a check question whose answer follows from the same model; each rung adds one idea.
sophisticationHooks: A geometric typeface of about 12 letters drawn in code from rectangles, circles and polygons, so area is computed exactly and no font file is used
Live white-area readout between neighbours inside the x-height zone, capped by depth
Blur slider to see grey tone before and after spacing
Kerning pair editor that shows when area equalisation has run out
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: glyph set as SVG paths, area-between-glyphs routine (raster on an offscreen canvas, fixed resolution), five demos, three check questions with computed answers, intro and glossary. Cut: real font loading, full alphabet, export of a font, language-specific rules. The blur test is a plain canvas blur shown as a demonstration; the even-grey goal is not cited as fact.
risks: Area equalisation is a simplified model of a judgement-based craft; the page must say it is a model and that real fonts are finished by eye.

The definitions of kerning and tracking and the claim that they are often confused are unverified (one result, blended summaries); the page defines the terms in its own words and shows 'as of 2026-10-13, per LS Graphics' or omits the confusion claim.

The A, L, T, V, W, Y trap-space claim and the even-grey goal are unverified; the page shows them as 'as reported by FontShop' or leaves them out, and the pair demos stand on the page's own computed areas.
The page must not name tools or foundries as endorsements; the method is described in its own words and credited generically.
Spacing is partly perceptual, so the lesson must show measured area honestly as a model and avoid claiming a single correct spacing.
Hand-drawn geometric glyphs may space oddly under the area rule; builders need a quick eyeball pass on the AVOID demo before polish.

verification.notes: The core claim (sidebearings first, kerning for leftovers, n-fence, x-height zone) is confirmed by independent results; definitional and confusion claims stay unverified and are softened. A code-drawn 12-letter typeface with a raster area routine fits one morning, and the idea is delightful if the draggable demos feel tactile.
